title: PitchBench: Measuring Pitch Hearing in Audio-Language Models
claim: The benchmark is a structured taxonomy of tasks, organized by level and category, spanning simple to complex perception.
layout: Central pyramid with task lists on left and right, color-coded by category
description: A central pyramid is split into three levels. The bottom level is a grey base labelled A1 Single pitch, with A2 Loudness and A3 Duration above it. The middle level is cut into four vertical colored wedges: B Temporal in blue, C Chord in lavender, D Sequence in green and E Acoustic in tan. A small teal triangle labelled F sits at the top. Task lists flank the pyramid. The left side lists A, B, C and F with their subtasks (A1–A3, B1–B5, C1–C4, F1–F2), each under a bracketed level label: Level 1 Atomic, Level 2 Contextual, Level 3 Polyphonic. The right side lists D1–D8 and E1–E6. Each category's headers and codes use the same color as its pyramid region. The eye goes first to the pyramid, then to the lists.
caption: PitchBench: 28 tasks across 3 levels and 6 categories, covering atomic, contextual, and polyphonic pitch perception.
abstract: Audio-language models (ALMs) are increasingly used in real-world applications that require music understanding, including tutoring, captioning, recommendation, and production. Yet existing benchmarks rarely evaluate a fundamental component of this understanding: pitch hearing. Pitch underpins the identification of notes, chords, and melodies and the grounding of captions in musical events, but it remains unclear how reliably ALMs perceive fine-grained pitch across sound sources, acoustic conditions, and response formats. We introduce PitchBench, an evaluation suite comprising 28 tasks that assess absolute and relative pitch perception under variations in loudness, note duration, sound source, time stretching, background noise, and other acoustic conditions. Tasks range from identifying isolated pitches to tracking voices in four-part musical textures. Evaluating frontier ALMs, we find that pitch hearing remains highly unreliable. Models perform poorly across settings, with accuracy varying sharply depending on the notation or prompt format, indicating instruction drift. Specialized DSP and neural pitch baselines achieve mean scores of approximately 73.2% and 75.2%, respectively, compared with approximately 53.9% for the strongest ALM. We release PitchBench as an evaluation benchmark, a training dataset, and a Python package with data generation tools to support future research on pitch-aware audio-language modeling.
